title: Acute Eye Problems Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing acute eye problems including red eye and eye pain, distinguishing vision-threatening conditions from benign causes, and supporting safe triage and urgent referral.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace ophthalmology examination or urgent referral when serious pathology is suspected.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Acute angle-closure glaucoma (severe pain, red eye, vision loss, halos, headache).
Corneal ulcer or keratitis (pain, photophobia, reduced vision, discharge).
Acute iritis or uveitis (pain, photophobia, red eye, visual symptoms).
Retinal detachment (floaters, flashing lights, visual field loss).
Chemical or thermal burn (history of exposure, pain, reduced vision).
Acute eye injury or hyphema (trauma, blood in anterior chamber).
Acute scleritis (severe pain, red patch, vision-threatening).
Giant-cell arteritis with vision loss (age >50, systemic symptoms).
items.importantLimitation: Red eye does not always mean infection; serious non-infectious causes can masquerade as conjunctivitis.

sections.title: Focused history
sections.intro: Characterise onset, symptoms and risk factors to guide diagnosis.

items.title: Symptom characteristics
mustConfirmOrExclude: Onset: sudden vs. gradual; unilateral or bilateral.
Pain: severity (0-10), location (surface vs. deep), triggered by light or eye movement?
Vision: clear or blurred; any loss or floaters?
Red eye: where (generalised redness vs. localised patch)?
Discharge: colour, consistency; crusty on waking?
Photophobia, watering or foreign body sensation?

items.title: Red-flag features in history
mustConfirmOrExclude: Sudden severe pain (suggests acute glaucoma, scleritis or keratitis).
Vision loss or visual blurring (suggests corneal, retinal or optic nerve pathology).
Floaters and flashing lights (suggests retinal detachment or posterior uveitis).
Recent trauma or chemical/thermal exposure.
Photophobia with pain (suggests uveitis, keratitis or acute glaucoma).
Recent eye surgery or contact lens use.
Known glaucoma, uveitis or autoimmune disease.
Age >50 with vision loss and systemic symptoms (GCA).

items.title: Exposure and risk factors
mustConfirmOrExclude: Trauma: direct blow, scratch, contact lens trauma, foreign body.
Chemical or thermal exposure: acid splash, alkali exposure, UV exposure.
Recent eye surgery, steroid use or systemic disease (TB, syphilis, sarcoid).
Sexually transmitted infections (chlamydia, gonorrhoea).
Immunosuppression (increased risk of unusual infections or malignancy).

sections.title: Vision-threatening conditions screen
sections.intro: Positive features should trigger urgent same-day ophthalmology referral.

items.title: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
urgentFeatures: Sudden onset severe unilateral eye pain and redness.
Blurred vision with halos around lights.
Fixed mid-dilated pupil; hazy cornea.
Elevated intraocular pressure (>40 mmHg if measured).
Nausea and vomiting may accompany ocular symptoms.
implications: Urgent same-day ophthalmology assessment to lower IOP and prevent blindness.

items.title: Corneal ulcer or keratitis
urgentFeatures: Pain, photophobia and watering.
Vision blurring or reduced.
Discharge (purulent in bacterial infection).
White infiltrate or opacity on cornea.
Risk factors: contact lens use, recent eye trauma, corneal scarring, immunosuppression.
implications: Urgent same-day ophthalmology referral; do not delay due to infection risk.

items.title: Acute anterior uveitis or iritis
urgentFeatures: Unilateral eye pain and photophobia.
Ciliary redness (redness at corneal edge).
Anterior chamber reaction (white cell inflammation).
Small irregular pupil, posterior synechiae.
May follow trauma or be associated with systemic disease.
implications: Urgent ophthalmology referral; treatment needed to prevent vision loss and glaucoma.

items.title: Retinal detachment
urgentFeatures: Floaters and photopsia (flashing lights).
Progressive shadow or visual field defect.
Pain usually absent (suggests detachment rather than uveitis).
Risk factors: high myopia, prior eye surgery, family history, trauma.
implications: Urgent same-day ophthalmology referral to prevent permanent vision loss.

items.title: Chemical or thermal burn
urgentFeatures: History of chemical splash, alkali, acid or thermal exposure.
Severe pain, redness and reduced vision.
Corneal opacification or eyelid burn.
Chemosis or subconjunctival haemorrhage.
implications: Urgent same-day ophthalmology assessment; aggressive eye irrigation may have already been done.

items.title: Acute scleritis
urgentFeatures: Severe deep eye pain (disproportionate to findings).
Localised area of scleral redness and swelling.
Vision may be affected.
Often associated with systemic disease (RA, vasculitis).
implications: Urgent ophthalmology referral; may indicate systemic disease requiring investigation.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Assess visual acuity, pupil response and anterior eye structures.

items.title: Visual acuity
howToTest: Test each eye separately using Snellen chart or near vision card.
Note if corrective lenses improve vision.
Assess ability to count fingers or detect light if vision severely reduced.
normal: 6/6 vision or baseline vision in affected eye.
abnormal: Any reduction from baseline; inability to count fingers or see light suggests serious pathology.
implications: Reduced vision suggests corneal, uveal, retinal or optic nerve pathology requiring urgent referral.

items.title: Pupil and light response
howToTest: Assess pupil size, equality and shape.
Test direct and consensual light reflex.
Assess for relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD): swinging torch test.
normal: Equal round pupils; brisk light response; no RAPD.
abnormal: Irregular pupil, sluggish response, mid-dilated fixed pupil, RAPD.
implications: Fixed mid-dilated pupil suggests acute glaucoma; RAPD suggests optic nerve pathology.

items.title: Cornea and anterior chamber
howToTest: Use bright light and magnification to examine cornea.
Look for clarity, infiltrates, ulcers, opacification or scarring.
Assess anterior chamber depth and clarity.
Fluorescein staining to detect epithelial defects.
normal: Clear cornea without infiltrate or ulcer; clear anterior chamber.
abnormal: White infiltrate, ulceration, opacification, hyphema or shallow chamber.
implications: Corneal infiltrate or ulcer requires urgent referral; hyphema suggests trauma; shallow chamber suggests angle-closure risk.

items.title: Conjunctiva and sclera
howToTest: Examine for redness pattern: diffuse vs. localised, ciliary vs. conjunctival.
Look for subconjunctival haemorrhage, chemosis or swelling.
Examine sclera for patches of redness or ischaemia.
normal: Clear or minimally injected conjunctiva; white sclera.
abnormal: Diffuse conjunctival redness (infection), ciliary redness (uveitis), subconjunctival haemorrhage, scleral patch (scleritis).
implications: Ciliary redness suggests uveitis; scleral patch suggests scleritis; subconjunctival haemorrhage may indicate trauma or bleeding disorder.

items.title: Fundal examination
howToTest: Dilate pupil if safe (after excluding narrow angles).
Examine optic disc: colour, cup, margins.
Examine periphery: look for retinal detachment, haemorrhage, exudates.
normal: Pink optic disc with clear margins, normal cup-to-disc ratio; intact macula; attached retina.
abnormal: Pallor or swelling of disc, retinal detachment, haemorrhage, exudates, pigmentation changes.
implications: Retinal detachment requires urgent referral; optic disc swelling suggests raised ICP or optic neuritis.

sections.title: Common clinical patterns
sections.intro: Pattern recognition supports safe triage and appropriate referral.

items.title: Viral conjunctivitis
commonFindings: Unilateral or bilateral redness and watering.
implications: Self-limiting; supportive care. Avoid eye patch. Contagious; advise hand hygiene.

items.title: Bacterial conjunctivitis
commonFindings: Purulent discharge; eyes sticky on waking.
implications: Topical antibiotics indicated. If gonorrhoea or chlamydia suspected, systemic treatment needed.

items.title: Allergic conjunctivitis
commonFindings: Seasonal pattern or identifiable allergen exposure.
Giant papillae on upper lid (in chronic cases).
No discharge or clear watery discharge.
implications: Allergen avoidance, topical antihistamines. Topical steroids for acute exacerbations.

items.title: Subconjunctival haemorrhage
commonFindings: Painless bright red patch under conjunctiva.
Often follows minor trauma or coughing.
implications: Reassurance; self-limiting. Investigate if traumatic, recurrent or associated with anticoagulation.

items.title: Dry eye syndrome
commonFindings: Worse in dry environments or with screen use.
implications: Artificial tears, lid hygiene, environmental modifications. Refer if severe or refractory.

sections.title: Management and disposition
sections.intro: Base decisions on vision-threat assessment and urgent referral criteria.

items.title: Investigation
mustConfirmOrExclude: Tonometry: measure intraocular pressure if acute glaucoma suspected.
Fluorescein: stain cornea to identify epithelial defects, ulcers or abrasion.
Slit-lamp examination: refer for assessment if not available.
Gonioscopy: assess angle if narrow-angle glaucoma risk.

items.title: Community management is appropriate when
mustConfirmOrExclude: No vision-threatening condition identified.
Vision normal or at baseline.
Likely diagnosis is viral or allergic conjunctivitis, subconjunctival haemorrhage or dry eye.
Patient reliable for follow-up.

items.title: Urgent same-day ophthalmology referral
urgentFeatures: Reduced vision or vision loss.
Severe eye pain (suggests glaucoma, scleritis, keratitis, uveitis or burns).
Floaters with flashing lights (retinal detachment).
White infiltrate, ulcer or opacity on cornea.
Mid-dilated fixed pupil or hazy cornea.
Subconjunctival haemorrhage after significant trauma.
Chemical or thermal burn.
implications: Same-day or emergency ophthalmology assessment required to preserve vision.

items.title: Acute eye problems
safetyNetting: Go to ED or call 999 immediately for: chemical or thermal exposure to eye; severe eye trauma with vision loss; eye injury with blood in eye; or signs of globe rupture.

Contact eye services urgently (same-day) for: sudden vision loss; severe eye pain with redness; floaters and flashing lights suggesting retinal detachment; corneal ulcer or keratitis; or eye injury affecting vision.
Speak to your GP or eye service if: red eye or discharge is not improving after 5-7 days of treatment; you are having recurrent eye infections; or you have concerns about your vision.
